content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"The fear of the LORD is reverent awe and worshipful respect toward God—rather than mere terror—that constitutes the beginning of wisdom and expresses itself in obedience to his commandments, covenant loyalty, and hatred/avoidance of evil (Prov 1:7; 9:10; Eccl 12:13; Job 28:28; Prov 8:13).","book_summary":"Reverent awe expressed as keeping the commandments and departing from evil, anchored to Ecclesiastes 12:13.","consensus_core_identification":"Reverent awe of God producing obedience and turning from evil, foundational to wisdom.","book_core_identification":"Reverent awe of God expressed concretely in commandment-keeping and departure from evil.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book compresses the consensus into its behavioral expression (obedience and shunning evil), which the consensus itself explicitly includes (Deut 10:12; Eccl 12:13; Prov 8:13; Job 28:28). It omits the 'beginning of wisdom' framing and the filial/servile and dread-of-judgment nuances, but omission of subsidiary emphases is not a boundary change.","material_contradiction":"None. The book affirms exactly what all four consensus responses give as the primary meaning: reverent awe worked out in obedience and moral avoidance of evil.","rationale":"All four blind responses identify the fear of the LORD as reverent awe joined to obedience and the shunning of evil, citing Ecclesiastes 12:13 among their primary bases. The book's entry is a terse restatement of that same identification—awe expressed as keeping commandments and departing from evil—corresponding to Eccl 12:13 and Job 28:28/Prov 8:13. There is no re-identification, narrowing, or added condition that would exclude cases the consensus admits; the differences are compression and emphasis only.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book's definition, by casting fear wholly as behavioral expression (commandment-keeping) rather than including any element of genuine dread or the wisdom-foundation motif, slightly narrows the semantic range some consensus responses preserve, which might suggest REFINED. But the consensus responses themselves treat the covenant-obedience expression as part of the primary meaning, so this is emphasis, not boundary change. Also, the single printed citation (Eccl 12:13) supports 'keeping the commandments' but not explicitly 'departing from evil,' which is why support is only partial.","confidence":"high"}
